articles.expand: Citi’s shift removes one of the last prominent holdouts against a December hike, so the debate moves from whether the Fed tightens again to when. The swing in October pricing, which spiked after the data and then faded, shows traders are uncertain about the timing and are likely to react strongly to any Fed speaker who leans either way before the meeting. A higher-for-longer path, with cuts pushed out to mid-2027, tends to support the US dollar and Treasury yields and to weigh on rate-sensitive assets. articles.title: Fed’s Daly: more rate hikes likely needed, but no urgency to move in October
articles.expand: Daly’s comments are the clearest pushback yet against the jump in October hike pricing that followed the CPI data. Expect them to trim the odds of a move on October 27-28 without denting expectations for a December increase. That mix would ease some pressure on the front end of the Treasury curve while leaving longer-dated yields anchored to a higher-for-longer outlook. Because Daly linked headline inflation directly to gasoline prices, oil remains the key swing factor. A further surge in crude tied to the Iran war would test her view that the Fed can afford to wait. Her remarks also contrast ...

articles.title: Fed catch up - Goolsbee calls CPI discouraging as Beige Book flags diesel-fuelled price pressure
articles.expand: Together, the two releases make an October hike harder to dismiss. Markets are pricing close to a 40% chance of a move on October 27-28, even though key officials had steered expectations toward December. The oil link is central: diesel costs from the Iran war now run through freight, farming and airfares, which raises the risk of second-round effects the Fed cannot easily look through. That supports Treasury yields at the front end and the US dollar, and keeps mortgage rates under upward pressure. Further strength in crude or diesel would add weight to the case for moving sooner. Next week’s ...

articles.title: Australia jobs preview: NAB sees 20,000 gain, unemployment steady at 4.6%
articles.expand: With NAB, Westpac and consensus all at 20,000 and three major banks seeing unemployment at 4.6%, the bar for a surprise sits mainly in the jobless rate. A drop to 4.5% would revive the case for further RBA tightening and could support the Australian dollar and short-dated yields. A rise to 4.7% would push the other way, adding weight to the view that four hikes are already doing enough.
